content: Cryptosporidium Cryptosporidium is an obligate intracellular coccidian parasite with a complex life cycle that includes both sexual and asexual reproduction. Thick-walled oocysts, measuring 4–6 µm in diameter, are excreted in feces. The genus Cryptosporidium comprises approximately 13 species, with human infections primarily caused by C. hominis and the cattle genotype of C. parvum. Other species of Cryptosporidium have been reported to cause infections less frequently. Cryptosporidium was first identified as a human pathogen in 1976, and waterborne transmission was confirmed in 1984. Human Health Effects Cryptosporidium typically causes self-limiting diarrhea, which may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and fever. In healthy individuals, symptoms usually resolve within a week but can persist for a month or longer. The severity of cryptosporidiosis varies depending on age and immune status. In severely immunocompromised individuals, the infection can be life-threatening. Outbreaks of cryptosporidiosis can have significant public health and socioeconomic impacts due to the large number of individuals affected. Source and Occurrence A wide range of animals serve as reservoirs for C. hominis and C. parvum, with humans and livestock, particularly young animals, being the most significant sources of human infections. Calves can excrete up to 10¹⁰ oocysts per day. Oocysts have been detected in raw sewage at concentrations as high as 14,000 per liter and in surface water at 5,800 per liter. They can survive for weeks to months in freshwater environments. Cryptosporidium oocysts have been identified in many drinking-water supplies, but the presence of human-infectious species is not always confirmed. Current analytical techniques provide indirect measures of viability and do not indicate human infectivity. Oocysts are also found in recreational waters. Routes of Exposure Cryptosporidium is transmitted via the fecal-oral route, with person-to-person contact being the primary mode of infection. Other sources include the consumption of contaminated food and water, as well as direct contact with infected farm animals or domestic pets. Contaminated drinking water and recreational water have been implicated in outbreaks. The largest recorded waterborne outbreak occurred in Milwaukee, USA, in 1993, infecting over 400,000 people. Studies have shown that ingestion of fewer than 10 oocysts can result in infection. Significance in Drinking Water The role of drinking water in the transmission of Cryptosporidium, including in large outbreaks, is well established. Oocysts are highly resistant to oxidizing disinfectants such as chlorine. However, UV light irradiation has been shown to inactivate oocysts effectively. Within a water safety plan, control measures should focus on preventing contamination of source water by human and livestock waste, ensuring adequate treatment, and protecting water during distribution. Due to their small size, oocysts are challenging to remove using conventional filtration processes, requiring well-designed and well-operated systems. Membrane filtration processes may offer an effective alternative for oocyst removal. Because of their resistance to disinfectants, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms cannot reliably indicate the presence or absence of Cryptosporidium oocysts in drinking water supplies. Cyclospora cayetanensis Cyclospora cayetanensis is a single-celled, obligate intracellular coccidian protozoan parasite belonging to the family Eimeriidae. It produces thick-walled oocysts, measuring 8–10 µm in diameter, which are excreted in the feces of infected individuals. Cyclospora is considered an emerging waterborne pathogen. Human Health Effects When ingested, sporozoites are released from the oocysts and invade epithelial cells in the small intestine. Clinical symptoms of cyclosporiasis include watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, weight loss, anorexia, myalgia, and occasionally vomiting and fever. Relapsing illness is common. Source and Occurrence Humans are the only known host for Cyclospora. Unsporulated oocysts are excreted in feces and undergo sporulation in the environment, which takes 7–12 days depending on environmental conditions. Only sporulated oocysts are infectious. Cyclospora has been detected in sewage and water sources, but there is limited information on its prevalence in water environments due to the lack of quantification techniques. Routes of Exposure Cyclospora is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. Person-to-person transmission is unlikely because oocysts must sporulate outside the host to become infectious. Primary routes of exposure include contaminated water and food. Foodborne outbreaks have been linked to the consumption of crops irrigated with contaminated water. Drinking water has also been implicated in outbreaks, such as one in Chicago, USA, in 1990, where infections were associated with tap water potentially contaminated by stagnant water from a rooftop reservoir. Significance in Drinking Water Cyclospora oocysts are resistant to disinfection and are not inactivated by standard chlorination practices. Control measures within a water safety plan should include preventing source water contamination by human waste, followed by adequate treatment and protection of water during distribution. Due to the resistance of the cysts to disinfectants, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms cannot reliably indicate the presence or absence of Cyclospora in drinking water supplies. Entamoeba histolytica Entamoeba histolytica is the most prevalent intestinal protozoan pathogen worldwide and belongs to the superclass Rhizopoda in the subphylum Sarcodina. It has a feeding, replicative trophozoite stage (10–60 µm in diameter) and a dormant cyst stage (10–20 µm in diameter) that develops under unfavorable conditions. Infection occurs through the ingestion of cysts. Genetic differences between pathogenic and non-pathogenic strains have been identified, with the latter reclassified as E. dispar. Human Health Effects Approximately 85–95% of infections with E. histolytica are asymptomatic. Acute intestinal amoebiasis has an incubation period of 1–14 weeks. Clinical disease results from the penetration of epithelial cells in the gastrointestinal tract by amoebic trophozoites. Around 10% of infected individuals develop dysentery or colitis, characterized by diarrhea with cramping, lower abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and the presence of blood and mucus in the stool. Trophozoites may invade other organs, such as the liver, lungs, and brain, sometimes with fatal outcomes. Source and Occurrence Humans are the primary reservoir of infection, with no significant animal reservoirs identified. During the acute phase of infection, patients excrete only trophozoites, which are not infectious. Cysts can remain viable in aquatic environments for several months at low temperatures. Waterborne transmission is more common in tropical regions, where carrier rates can exceed 50%, compared to temperate regions, where prevalence is generally below 10%. Routes of Exposure Person-to-person contact and contamination of food by infected food handlers are significant transmission routes. Contaminated water and the consumption of crops irrigated with contaminated water also play substantial roles. Sexual transmission, particularly among male homosexuals, has been documented. Significance in Drinking Water The transmission of E. histolytica through contaminated drinking water has been confirmed. Cysts are relatively resistant to disinfection and may not be inactivated by standard chlorination practices. Control measures should focus on preventing source water contamination by human waste, followed by adequate treatment and protection of water during distribution. Due to the resistance of the cysts to disinfectants, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms cannot reliably indicate the presence or absence of E. histolytica in drinking water supplies. Giardia intestinalis Giardia spp. are flagellated protozoa that parasitize the gastrointestinal tract of humans and certain animals. Human infection, known as giardiasis, is typically caused by G. intestinalis (also known as G. lamblia or G. duodenalis). Giardia has a simple life cycle, consisting of a flagellated trophozoite that multiplies in the gastrointestinal tract and an infectious thick-walled cyst that is intermittently shed in large numbers in feces. Human Health Effects Giardia has been recognized as a human parasite for over 200 years. After ingestion and excystation, trophozoites attach to the surfaces of the gastrointestinal tract. Infections may be asymptomatic, particularly in children, where up to 20% may carry Giardia without symptoms. Symptoms of giardiasis include diarrhea and abdominal cramps. Severe cases may involve malabsorption deficiencies in the small intestine, particularly in young children. Giardiasis is self-limiting in most cases but can become chronic, lasting over a year in some individuals. Studies have shown that ingestion of fewer than 10 cysts can result in infection. Source and Occurrence Giardia can multiply in a wide range of animal species and humans, which excrete cysts into the environment. Cysts have been detected in sewage and contaminated water sources, with concentrations as high as 88,000 per liter.
